articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Stock Slides After Huang Apologizes for Affair With Alleged Spy
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

articles.title_orig: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.title_zh: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.content_orig:
The Odyssey, the "forever cruise" left stranded in Southeast Asia after its owner struggled with financial problems , has been held by authorities in Singapore, according to court records obtained by CBS News.
A Singaporean law firm, Helmsman LLC, is listed as the solicitor in the "arrest" of the ship, but it is unclear whom the firm is representing. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News it is likely a fuel supplier.
"The vessel has been placed under arrest pursuant to a court order," Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said in a statement cited by the French news agency AFP and other outlets on Monday. "The crew onboard are reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors. There are no passengers on board."
It added that the ship was "anchored in Singapore port waters." AFP described the ship as being "impounded" by Singaporean authorities.
The luxury cruise ship is currently being operated by its lender after its owner, Villa Vie Residences, couldn't keep up with payments.
Villa Vie owes one supplier in the area approximately $500,000, though it's unclear whether that supplier hired the law firm to solicit the arrest.
A ship arrest is a legal process in Singapore in which a vessel can be detained or seized following a legal claim.
The journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship, launched in October 2024, came to a sudden end last month in Cambodia, where residents on the ship had just hours to disembark.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, these details included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
AFP cited Villa Vie Residences as saying "extraordinary increases" in the cost of fuel amid the U.S. war with Iran had driven its monthly fuel expenses from about $1,800 per guest cabin, to as much as $8,000 in some parts of Asia, where many nations rely heavily on imports from the Persian Gulf.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:24 p.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats
articles.title_zh: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats

By RYAN HOOPER, CRIME CORRESPONDENT and NICK MIAO
Published: 07:27 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 09:46 EST, 9 November 2026
A former teacher who claimed to be an ex-IRA member has been jailed after sending racist death threats to Kemi Badenoch .
In one of several emails sent last year, Kieran Kyle told the Tory leader 'I would have shot you dead' days after she posted a social media video referencing Bloody Sunday.
And in response to the Conservative Party leader's Parliament email address, the former secondary-school teacher wrote: 'When I was in the IRA I would have shot you f****** dead.'
Mrs Badenoch and her husband, Hamish, were said to have been left 'distressed' and 'very upset' by Kyle's correspondence – but told the court their wider concerns were the attacks on public figures 'which undermine a healthy democracy'.
Kyle, 43, from Gillingham in Kent, claimed he was not aware of who Mrs Badenoch was at the time of the offensive emails.
He was handed a 20-week jail term after he pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature at Westminster Magistrates' Court this afternoon.
Prosecutor Ben Holt said: 'In interview he admitted to sending the messages using the most distressing language possible, to cause the most distress possible.
'There is some planning from Mr Kyle with what language will be used to cause distress. Plainly, this offending was deliberate.'
Kieran Kyle, from Gillingham in Kent, admitted sending offensive emails to Kemi Badenoch and her husband
Kyle also sent emails containing death threats and racial slurs to Mrs Badenoch's husband on April 28 and 29.
He warned Mr Badenoch that his wife was 'misusing Bloody Sunday' and said: 'Pray she never ends up in Belfast, cos she will be left face down in a ditch with a bullet in her head.'
Three further messages sent to Mrs Badenoch's official email were received by the head of her parliamentary office, Cheryl Bacon – one of which used an extreme racial slur.
In her victim impact statement, Mrs Badenoch said: 'Our primary concern arising from this offence is not the personal impact on us but the wider consequences that malicious communications and targeted harassment have on our democratic life.
'When individuals choose to intimidate, threaten, or aggressively target elected representatives or public figures, the harm extends far beyond any single person. It undermines a healthy democracy.
'Public service relies on people being willing to step forward, often at significant personal cost, to represent their communities and contribute to public life.
'Increasingly, however, those who do so face hostility, harassment and attempts to silence or intimidate them. This behaviour creates an environment in which fewer capable people feel able to participate.
'It narrows the pool of those willing to stand for office, reduces diversity of thought and background, and ultimately weakens the quality of governance available to the public.'
The emails sent to Tory leader Mrs Badenoch and her husband Hamish left the couple 'distressed' and 'very upset', the court heard
In her statement, read by Mr Holt, she added: 'Malicious communication is not simply unpleasant, it is corrosive.
'It fosters a climate in which political debate becomes dominated by fear rather than ideas, and where individuals - regardless of party or ideology - must weigh their desire to serve against the risk of becoming a target.
'When harassment becomes normalised, democratic institutions suffer. Decision-making becomes more cautious, public engagement declines and trust in the political process erodes.
'The offence committed here contributes to that wider pattern. It reinforces a culture in which public figures are treated as legitimate targets for abuse rather than as individuals performing roles essential to the functioning of society.
'The impact is cumulative: each incident adds to an atmosphere that discourages participation and undermines the integrity of public life.
'We are therefore making this statement not about our own personal distress, which does exist, but the larger harm to the body politic.'
She said harassing politicians and public figures 'damages our democracy, deters good people from entering public service, and diminishes the quality of leadership available to all of us'.
'That is the real impact of this offence, and it is why addressing such behaviour matters,' she said.
Defending, Baiju Thittala said Kyle was a schoolteacher for around ten years but his mental health deteriorated after he was threatened with being stabbed by a student in 2023.
A knife was later found in the student's backpack, the court heard.
Mr Thittala said: 'From that point onwards, Mr Kyle's mental health started to decline.'
He said Kyle, who has a nine-year-old son, lost his job as a media teacher at Knole Academy in Sevenoaks after 'oppressive management' took over the school.
Mr Thittala added that, at the time of the offences, Kyle was at a low point in his mental health and the malicious emails were an 'impulsive, emotional reaction'.
In a back and forth over Kyle's claims he did not know who Mrs Badenoch was at the time of the emails, District Judge Sam Goozee said the claim 'is something I struggled with, because he chose to email her parliamentary office'.
Mr Thittala replied: 'He Googled [Mrs Badenoch's name] and it came up as the Opposition leader.'
Judge Goozee said: 'But he emailed her husband first… In time, he located Mr Badenoch's address, which wasn't in the public record.
'So he clearly knew who Mrs Badenoch was, because he knew how to research to locate Mr Badenoch's email address.'
The defence barrister spoke to Kyle briefly and then told the judge: 'He was not clearly aware who he was sending it to.'
The judge said: 'Mr Kyle is an experienced school teacher and he did not know who Mrs Badenoch was at the time he sent the message?'
Mr Thittala said: 'Yes… he Googled it, he sent the message. He didn't even know who he sent it to.'
Sentencing, the judge said: 'The actions were deliberate and, in my assessment, there is a high level of culpability.
'Impulsiveness may explain a single email but not the several you sent. It was targeted.
'This is not just an isolated email, it was several emails to her parliamentary office and her husband in a short period of time.'
He said he did not find Kyle's explanation 'credible', adding the behaviour 'undermines democratic processes and how politicians run their everyday lives'.
The judge added: 'Mrs Badenoch was providing a public service at the time of the offence as a member of parliament and leader of the Conservative party.
'As I have stated from the outset, these offences, targeted at a member of parliament to cause fear, undermine the fabric of the democratic process and affect how politicians conduct their day-to-day lives.
'Your emails included threats to kill… the harm you caused to Mrs Badenoch was significant, as well as her husband and secondary harm to her staff.'
Kyle showed no emotion as he was jailed.
Judge Goozee also imposed a five-year restraining order against contacting Mrs Badenoch, her husband or her staff. He also ordered a surcharge of £154.
Earlier this year, Mrs Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being used in a social media clip to criticise a bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.
The Conservative leader said she did not sign off on the video and that it was sent out by 'very young people'.

All four come in a redesigned 38mm stainless steel case that measures 44.75mm lug to lug and 11.5mm thick. It also carries Awake’s new brand identity: a handwritten logo that first appeared in May with the Sơn Mài Guilloché collection and continues here.
As is now becoming a signature for the brand, the dials come out of a lacquer workshop in Hanoi, and they take time. Each one takes more than ten hours to apply and polish roughly twelve layers of pigmented lacquer over sheets of silver leaf. Awake says that limits it to about 100 dials per year for each permanent model.
Awake has also become known for its use of lume. The Chiaroscuro luminous signature flips the usual approach, with sculpted steel caps set over blocks of Super-LumiNova BGW9 instead of lume painted onto the markers and hands.
Inside is the La Joux-Perret G101 automatic, which offers a 68-hour power reserve and now sits under a new tungsten rotor. The case is good for 100 meters of water resistance. Every watch ships on a Jean Rousseau and Bouveret strap handcrafted in France, in alcantara or nubuck lined with rubberized calfskin. The straps feature quick-release spring bars and the new Fitwell M1 micro-adjustable pin buckle.
The Awake Sơn Mài Silver Leaf collection retails for €2,640 (around $2,950 USD) including VAT. Deliveries start in late November.
I’ve had the pleasure of seeing Awake a few times over the last few months, first at Chronopolis in Geneva and then at Wind-Up in both Chicago and New York, and consistently, they have one of the most distinctive setups at these shows. The vibrant, deep colors and designs draw you in, and the story behind each dial keeps you there. With each dial being slightly unique, there’s something mesmerizing about looking (or taking out your loupe) deeper into the dial. Each is unmistakably Awake. And that tradition is pushed further here, in what is my favorite execution yet.
The Vignette styling is executed extremely well, and the scale of the gradient is just right, fading to black to make way for the indices. At 38mm this is sized very well indeed. Also, it must be said, if you haven’t seen these in person, make your way to the next Wind-Up, because the lume is my favorite part. It’s so unexpected and also executed with care. It doesn’t need to be there, which makes it even better that it’s included and executed this well.
It’s a lot of watch for less than $3,000 USD. Flip it over and Awake tells you exactly what it’s up to. The text around the movement reads “Illuminating the hands and heritage behind rare crafts.” Awake is doing that both literally and figuratively, and at a level well beyond what you’d expect from a brand this young.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 18e Could Feature Bigger Display and Battery
articles.title_zh: iPhone 18e Could Feature Bigger Display and Battery
articles.content_orig:
Apple's standard iPhone 18 and the lower-cost iPhone 18e will both feature 6.3-inch displays and use the same battery, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ."
In a new post on Weibo, the leaker shared an annotated, side-by-side diagram of the phones' purported internals, labeled "Taycan" for the ‌iPhone 18‌ and "Nevera" for the iPhone 18e. Fixed Focus Digital said the diagram was already circulating online and broadly matched what their sources had told them. They pointed to the battery as an example of the interchangeable parts they had previously described.
The diagram's annotations list a 4,430 mAh battery for both models. That would be an increase of about 21% from 3,671 mAh for the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and about 11% from 4,005 mAh for the iPhone 18e. The notes attribute the extra room in the standard model to changes to the bottom speaker and haptic engine. The diagram also shows two rear cameras on the standard ‌iPhone 18‌, including an Ultra Wide camera, and a single rear camera on the iPhone 18e, just like previous models.
A 6.3-inch display would be a noticeable step up from the 6.1-inch screen on the iPhone 17e . Fellow Weibo leaker "Digital Chat Station" previously claimed the iPhone 18e would retain a 6.12-inch OLED display at 60Hz , along with a single 48-megapixel rear camera and a potential upgrade to the front-facing camera. The same source expects the standard iPhone 18 to retain its 6.3-inch display with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz, along with a larger battery.
In an earlier post , Fixed Focus Digital said a new chip was the only iPhone 18e upgrade they could confirm at the time and suggested the two models would share some manufacturing processes.
Digital Chat Station expects the iPhone 18e to contain Apple's 2nm A20 chip, up from the 3nm A19 in the ‌iPhone 17e‌. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo has said Apple's lower-end spring 2027 iPhones will pair the A20 chip with 9GB of RAM , up from 8GB. Both models are also rumored to get Apple's C2 modem, which would replace the Snapdragon X80 in the iPhone 17 and the C1X in the ‌iPhone 17e‌.
The iPhone 18e is expected to launch in spring 2027 alongside the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and second-generation iPhone Air . The ‌iPhone 17e‌ launched at $599 with 256GB of storage , and it is unclear if it will get a price increase like other iPhone models.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla Are Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street With This $53 Billion Warning
articles.content_orig:
For the better part of the last four years, no catalyst has played a bigger role in lifting the broader market than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) . Whether it's AI-accelerating hardware or AI applications, an IDC report pegs this cumulative addressable opportunity at $22.5 trillion from 2025 to 2031.
Few companies have taken the AI bull by the horns more than Nvidia ( NVDA +2.77% ) , Palantir Technologies ( PLTR +3.48% ) , and Tesla ( TSLA +4.23% ) .
Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are the infrastructure backbone of AI-accelerated data centers. None of its competitors are particularly close to matching the compute capabilities of its multiple generations of GPUs.
Meanwhile, AI-driven software-as-a-service provider Palantir is a veritable blueprint for deploying AI applications. The company's Gotham platform assists the U.S. military with planning and overseeing missions.
Electric-vehicle maker Tesla is also an AI applications maven. AI is integral to the success of its full self-driving software and its Optimus humanoid robots.
Image source: Getty Images.
While this trio has thrived amid the AI infrastructure build-out, the individuals who know these companies best are sending all the wrong signals to Wall Street .
Though stock market analysts spend day after day studying the same industry and the companies that define it, no one understands Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla better than their respective insiders.
An " insider " is a high-ranking executive, board member, or beneficial owner of at least 10% of a company's outstanding shares who may possess nonpublic information. Anytime an insider buys or sells their company's stock, they're legally required to file Form 4 with regulators within two business days. This allows investors to track whether a company's insiders have been buying or selling.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/06/26
In the case of this powerhouse AI trio, insiders have been undeniable net sellers of their company's stock over the trailing five years:
Collectively, insiders at these companies have sold more than $52.7 billion more of their own company's stock than they've purchased since early November 2021.
There is, however, an asterisk that should accompany the above data. Since high-ranking executives and board members are often compensated in stock or options , they're required to sell some of their holdings to cover their federal and/or state tax liability. In other words, insider selling isn't automatically a bad thing -- especially if it's for tax purposes.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/06/26
What's equally unnerving, from an investment standpoint, is the relative lack of insider buying . With the exception of one sizable purchase totaling nearly $1 billion by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, insider buying has been practically nonexistent in this trio over the trailing five years:
If insiders aren't buying, historical precedent might explain why.
For more than 30 years, every game-changing innovation has navigated an early-innings bubble-bursting event. This includes the internet, 3D printing, blockchain technology, and the metaverse.
Stock market bubbles throughout history…

AI stocks now ~40% of the market. https://t.co/RxSAh09k6F
The reason these bubbles form and subsequently burst is that investors consistently overestimate the pace of optimization for game-changing technologies . While AI solutions have been welcomed with open arms, we're likely several years away from businesses optimizing these solutions to boost sales and profits. In other words, the door is wide open for a potential AI bubble-bursting event.

articles.content_orig:
By Fred Meintjes 2026-11-09T11:11:00+00:00
Tru-Cape says China’s new tariff deal for Africa is already benefitting South African exporters
The South African fruit business has said that while it has been able to grow exports to China under the country’s zero tariff deal for African countries, there is a short window of opportunity for it to negotiate a permanent trade deal.
The country’s apple exporters revealed this week that they have seen a significant increase in shipments to China.
“The removal of Chinese import tariffs on South African fruit is already delivering results for Tru-Cape Fruit Marketing, with the company’s apple exports to China increasing by almost 50 per cent year-to-date,” stated Tru-Cape Marketing.
”The development has created new opportunities to grow South African apples’ presence in one of the world’s largest consumer markets, while highlighting the need for more competitive market access in India.”
Previously, South African fruit entering China was subject to a 10 per cent import tariff.
The reduction to 0 per cent has levelled the playing field for Southern Hemisphere suppliers, giving South African exporters a more competitive position in the market.
This is likely to also provide further impetus for South African pear, table grape, stonefruit and citrus exporters.
“It is important that we secure a longer-term free trade agreements deal,” the Citrus Growers Association recently commented.
“The playing field is now definitely level, with all Southern Hemisphere countries enjoying a zero tariff,” noted Conrad Fick, marketing director at Tru-Cape.
Tru-Cape currently accounts for more than 20 per cent of South African apple exports to the market.
”South African Royal Gala Red and Royal Beaut apples are performing particularly well, and we are also seeing growing acceptance of the Flash Gala brand, which is helping to increase both volumes and prices,” said Fick.
The country’s stonefruit exporters are also looking forward to their first season in the Chinese market.
“We are particularly excited about building with Sugar Prunes which is already well accepted amongst Chinese consumers,” added Luhan Marais of Icon Fruit.

articles.content_orig:
The chief executive of one of the world's largest public corporations is facing an inquiry following reports he conducted an 'affair' with an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang serves as chief executive officer of Nvidia, presently ranked second only to Apple amongst the globe's largest publicly traded firms, and is reported to have acknowledged the affair.
The $4.5 trillion American technology giant initiated the independent inquiry after reports emerged that its founder and CEO had become the subject of a 'foreign intelligence effort', the Nvidia Board of Directors confirmed in a statement.
The New York Times referenced US intelligence officials who identified businesswoman Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese operative.
Jensen Huang has now acknowledged he was "unfaithful" to his wife and expressed remorse for the pain he has inflicted upon her and their children, according to subsequent reports.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's Board stated it possessed no grounds to suspect that company secrets or US national security had been jeopardised - and indicated Mr Huang remained committed to continuing his leadership of the business.
Nvidia ranks amongst the world's most valuable corporations and is regarded as pivotal to manufacturing the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with Mr Huang having led it for over three decades.
The announcement followed Mr Huang's admission to the board that he had been intimate with a Chinese business executive, whom US intelligence identified as collecting information for Beijing, The New York Times reported. Mr Huang issued an apology in a message to the firm, the Times reported.
"I was unfaithful to my wife," he said.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
Nvidia's board stated it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but confirmed its investigation would scrutinise all available evidence.
Mr Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to co-operating with it," the board said.
Mr Huang, 63, will continue as chief executive throughout the probe.
The Times disclosed last month that US intelligence services had uncovered that Mr Huang had formed a close association with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and chip purchaser, and concluded that she was passing intelligence straight to Beijing.
The pair are not related, the Times confirmed.
Alice Huang previously worked as a television journalist in China before rising to senior executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, which has emerged as one of Nvidia's largest clients in Southeast Asia.
Megaspeed purchased more than 4.8 billion US dollars (£3.6 billion) worth of Nvidia chips during the past two years, the Times reported.
In a statement issued in recent hours, the Nvidia Board announced: "The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.
"Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

articles.title_zh: EXPLAINER - Why is the world’s top chipmaker caught in a US-China spy row?
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions over allegations that a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had a romantic relationship was gathering intelligence for Beijing.
Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe United States national security or confidential information has been compromised.
Nevertheless, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said in a statement , adding that Jensen Huang fully backs the review.
After the revelations, Nvidia – whose market capitalisation of $4.5 trillion is higher than the gross domestic product (GDP) of Japan, the world’s fourth-largest economy – saw its stock price tumble by more than 4 percent in trading overnight into Monday.
The controversy erupted as Washington seeks to prevent China from obtaining advanced American semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most powerful artificial intelligence chips, as the US and China fiercely compete for AI supremacy.
So what do we know about the affair, and how will this impact US-China relations and the race for AI dominance?
The allegations first emerged in a New York Times investigation late last month, which reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited by Beijing to gather information about Nvidia’s chief executive and potentially influence the company’s chip sales to China.
However, the precise nature of the information she allegedly obtained, whether any sensitive material was passed to Beijing and how much Jensen Huang knew about the alleged operation remain unclear. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related despite sharing a last name.
The two were reportedly seen together at industry events, including a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology exhibition in 2025.
On Sunday, the Nvidia chief acknowledged his infidelity in a staff memo.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said.
However, in late October, Jensen Huang had told Bloomberg News that his interactions with Alice Huang were related to her company, Megaspeed, describing them as “completely normal and not unusual”.
Also known as Huang Le, Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed International, which provides computing infrastructure used to operate and train AI systems.
According to The New York Times, Megaspeed had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing about $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.
A profile of Alice Huang found in a Chinese investment database listed previous employment at HSBC and Chinese television broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV, according to the AFP news agency, which said it could not independently verify those details.
Alice Huang has not publicly responded to the espionage allegations, and her whereabouts are currently unknown.
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation overseen by a committee of directors and external legal counsel to determine whether its president and CEO was targeted by foreign intelligence.
The company said it had no reason to believe national security or its proprietary information had been compromised while expressing confidence in Jensen Huang’s leadership.
“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” it said, adding that Jensen Huang has pledged to cooperate with the investigation and continue leading the company.
However, the allegations have unsettled investors.
“It deals a blow to the cult of Huang that has taken over the chip world in recent years,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at Britain’s IG Group, a leading derivatives trading firm, told Al Jazeera, while adding that it was too early to determine whether this moment might prove a “major turning point” for Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
“If this turns into a broader congressional investigation, then the shares are likely to come under pressure,” Beauchamp added. “As we learned from the financial crisis [in 2008 and 2009], once you go looking for skeletons in a cupboard, you usually find them.”
Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison, who also works at Nvidia, cancelled a planned visit to South Korea for an Nvidia AI event amid the controversy.
US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over suspicions that the company helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips in violation of US export restrictions.
However, no criminal charges against Jensen Huang or Alice Huang have been reported. The controversy has prompted bipartisan pressure in Washington.
Republican lawmakers on Wednesday called on Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on November 18, arguing that the allegations raise serious questions about China’s potential access to sensitive US technology.
“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” Republican Congressmen John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford said in a statement.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has also demanded answers from Nvidia and called for stronger legislation to prevent advanced US technology from reaching China.
“NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers. And we need to pass bipartisan legislation we have ready to stop advanced American technology from going to China,” she said in a statement.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has defended Jensen Huang, describing him as an “honourable guy”.
Asked whether he should have acted after reportedly receiving an intelligence briefing about the allegations, Trump said, “No, I don’t think so.”
Meanwhile, ⁠⁠⁠⁠Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson ⁠⁠⁠⁠Guo Jiakun on Monday said the “so-called ⁠⁠⁠⁠Chinese spy ⁠⁠⁠⁠narrative” was unsubstantiated. “It is nothing but smears against China,” Guo added.
Jensen Huang, who is seen as a close adviser to Trump on the AI trade , has repeatedly pushed to loosen chip sales restrictions to China.
The scandal threatens to intensify tensions between Washington and Beijing over access to the powerful semiconductors needed to develop advanced AI systems. Semiconductors are needed to run nearly all electronics from smartphones to cars and military equipment.
Nvidia is a central player in that competition, supplying chips used by major US technology companies to train and operate AI models. It was until October 30 the most valuable company in the world.
“AI is now a technology that is really shaping national economies and GDPs, and safeguarding becomes even more serious. So protecting not only confidential secrets but also advancements for geopolitical reasons becomes even more important,” Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, told Al Jazeera.
Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China over national security concerns. Nvidia’s top-of-the-line Blackwell GPU chips are banned for export to China.
The US has also clarified that restrictions apply to Chinese-owned companies operating outside China amid concerns that overseas subsidiaries could provide a route around export controls.
However, in December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to China, marking a major easing of US export restrictions. The H200, while not Nvidia’s top chip, is roughly six times more powerful than the model previously approved for sale to China, the H20.

articles.title_zh: US Stocks Rise as Oil Drop Outweighs Nvidia Woes: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were higher early on Monday, with traders keeping a close eye on technology shares after last week's volatility, while awaiting the release of key inflation data and earnings from major AI companies this week.
S&P 500 futures rose 0.34%, while Nasdaq 100 futures were around 0.5% higher. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average led gains, adding 0.76%.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal AI-driven selloff, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite bounced 1.09% to 24,579.42 and the broad-market S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86. The blue-chip Dow , however, lost 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to settle at 51,285.73.
Broader investor sentiment remained cautious following a batch of stronger-than-expected jobs data. Additionally, concerns linger after the Democrats' strong midterm results, amid fears that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom.
The tech sector will also be focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. A proxy for Nvidia shares was lower by 2% over the last 24 hours in trading on Hyperliquid.
Liz Ann Sonders, Schwab Center for Financial Research chief investment strategist, noted that the Nasdaq and Nasdaq-100 are oversold, with heavy de-risking by traders. Thursday marked the biggest day of retail selling since the Covid pandemic, according to Vanda Research. Retail traders haven't been taking advantage of the selloff, Sonders said.
"Retail has not proven to be the dip buyers that they have been in the past," she told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Friday. "You saw a really heavy amount of net selling … we may not fully be washed out yet, but we'll have to see whether that retail trader at some point decides to step back in."
Sonders suggested that the next short-term focus should be on companies' adjustments to capex plans and expectations for future profit margins.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave, Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent selloff has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
On Monday, traders will get September wholesale inventories data at 10 a.m. ET. Take-Two Interactive Software, Occidental Petroleum, KKR, Constellation Energy and Skydance are scheduled to report quarterly earnings.
Over in Asia, markets were mostly up on Monday, with Taiwanese equities leading the rise. The Taiwan Weighted Index closed 4.94% up at 41,664.7, marking the largest one-day gain since 31 July.
The index was powered by gains in tech heavyweights Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Hon Hai Precision Industry — also known as Foxconn.
Investors in Asia are also assessing October inflation data out from China, with the producer price index hitting its highest in over four years at 5.7%, and consumer inflation coming in slower than expected at 0.7%.
Nvidia shares were down around 5% in premarket trading Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
The key question for investors will be whether Huang will remain as CEO, according to Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Ives said in a Sunday note.
European stocks got off to a mixed start on Monday, with the regional Stoxx 600 index opening lower before moving to a 0.4% gain by 8:20 a.m. in London.
Mining stocks popped 1.7% as gold and copper prices bounced back from last week's downturn.
Italian bank Unicredit was the top performer, up 4.7% after its third-quarter net profit rose by a record 24% year-on-year and as it prepares to take control of Germany's Commerzbank .

articles.title_orig: Passenger trains crash in Egypt, killing 7 and injuring 125, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Passenger trains crash in Egypt, killing 7 and injuring 125, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.
Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.
Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.
Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

articles.title_orig: China Producer Inflation Accelerates as Consumer Prices Cool
articles.title_zh: China Producer Inflation Accelerates as Consumer Prices Cool
articles.content_orig:
Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row.
The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters. The increase was driven by a sharp rise in prices in the mining and raw materials industries.
The increase was driven by very strong external demand, Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ."
Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases.
The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, came in at 0.8%, down from the 1% seen in the month before.
The rise in consumer prices were still held up by prices of gasoline, which was the largest contributor to the increase in prices, but this was offset by a sharper than expected fall in food prices, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the urban division at China's National Bureau of Statistics.
The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales.
The mainland Chinese CSI 300 index gained 0.56% after the data release.
Pinpoint's Zhang said that domestic demand has been rather weak due to the property market, and this is a key reason why inflation is not picking up in China "There's no clear sign of stabilization [in that sector] yet," he said, adding this was weighing on the household consumer confidence and local government revenue.
"So the the overall economic momentum has been weak and hasn't really seen [a] clear sign of recovery," Zhang explained.

Trump blamed the results for last week's stock market sell-off.
Democrats won several key races in the high-stakes midterm elections -- with ABC News projecting that Democrats will take control of the Senate and the House.
Attorney General Todd Blanche suggested in an interview Sunday that there could be investigations of Democrats pushing oversight probes into President Donald Trump's administration, despite no evidence that such calls could amount to criminal threats.
"It depends on what's said. So, yes, there could be," Blanche said in an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" program, when asked if there could be such investigations.
"You have free speech in this country. You are allowed to be critical of President Trump, of me, of this administration. But when the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration because somebody will come after them, at some point, you have to draw the line," Blanche said.
Blanche's comments follow Trump's social media post on Saturday directing the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who have previewed plans for aggressive oversight probes into administration officials following Tuesday's midterms.
-ABC News' Alexander Mallin
President Donald Trump continued to criticize the results of Tuesday's midterm elections, saying in a post to social media on Sunday that they represented a "giant step back in History" for the U.S. and blaming them for the past week's stock market sell-off.
"America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election -- Even the Stock Market, which has been a 'ROCKETSHIP' under 'TRUMP,' took a one day, 3 Trillion Dollar loss. But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!" Trump wrote.
President Donald Trump is claiming, without providing evidence, that Democratic leaders are sending "threatening" letters and messages to Republicans and that he is directing the Department of Justice to investigate this alleged "criminal act."
"Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders. By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" he wrote on his social media platform.
The president does not specify what "letters" he is referring to or how this would constitute a "criminal act." This allegation comes in a long post slamming Democrats for suggesting impeachment efforts of Cabinet members, with the president accusing them of "extortion" and insisting that his administration has not committed any wrongdoing.
"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process. This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this," Trump said.
This comes after Democrats reclaimed both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, prompting anticipation of new congressional oversight. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie is expected to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which could come as early as Monday.
Trump also claimed, without providing evidence, that Democrats are "threatening" Republican donors simply for their party affiliation, with the president referring to this as "weaponization."
Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman made her first public appearance Thursday night, giving her victory speech after incumbent Mayor Karen Bass conceded the Los Angeles mayor's race.
Raman spoke to a gaggle of reporters and unsuspecting patrons at the Original Farmer's Market, saying she's made amends with Bass and City Hall over phone calls and is now focused on gaining public trust.
Raman also paid tribute to the mayor and thanked her for her service. She mentioned she and Bass have agreed to a smooth transition of power and went on to add that she's committed to working in tandem with city council.
"No matter what happened during the campaign, that is in the past now. And all of us, every single member of that city council and I are here because we love Los Angeles and we know that we need to work together in order to address the challenges that we have ahead," she said.
Raman added that her priority is instilling public trust in city government.
"I want to tell every single Angeleno out there, I am going to work so hard. And everyone behind me is going to work so hard to earn your trust, to earn you trust, and to earn the trust. To earn the trust of everyone across this city and to make people believe in Los Angeles again, to make believe in its City Hall again."
-ABC News' Clarissa Gonzales

articles.title_orig: The Kremlin call: How talking to Putin exposed Europe’s deepest rift over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: The Kremlin call: How talking to Putin exposed Europe’s deepest rift over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Beneath the chandeliers and oil paintings of his Presidential Palace, Finland’s president Alexander Stubb sat down next to his old friend Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian prime minister, to call Vladimir Putin.
They hoped such a dramatic and direct intervention with Russia’s leader would demonstrate European resolve.
Instead, the conversation on a damp autumn morning in Helsinki triggered the biggest rift among Nordic allies since Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — and exposed Europe’s wider divisions over how to deal with Moscow at a pivotal moment in the push for peace.
As Russian and Ukrainian negotiators prepare for talks with Donald Trump’s envoys in Abu Dhabi this week, the fallout from the call is still reverberating across Europe. Governments are arguing over who should represent Europe in future negotiations and remain divided over a question at the heart of the debate: Does engaging Putin help deliver peace, or simply reward aggression?
Underlying European anxiety is another dilemma: Can America be trusted to broker a fair deal for them and most of all for Ukraine?
EU leaders will grapple with these questions at an informal summit in Dublin this week. Few involved expect them to agree.
In an interview with POLITICO in Oslo, Støre explained why he and Stubb decided to call a leader waging hybrid warfare on Europe and killing Ukrainian civilians with daily drone and missile strikes.
“We work closely with our European partners in supporting Ukraine, but the only voice reaching Moscow comes from Washington,” Støre said. “And you know, we have good and open relations with the American negotiators, with the American administration, but this [war] happens in Europe. And living month by month, thinking that this war will end by Europe not talking to Moscow, I think, is an illusion.”
Other countries sharing a border — and a history —  with Putin’s Russia profoundly disagree.
“Europe should not be in a mediator’s position,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO in another interview . “You should not take the role of trying to please the dictator.”
Based on interviews with politicians, diplomats and officials, many granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, this is the inside story of a phone call that shook Europe.
Europe has struggled for influence over the stop-start Ukraine peace process ever since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, promptly picked up the phone to Putin and ended U.S. financial assistance to Kyiv.
Trump’s interventions shattered the transatlantic consensus built under his predecessor Joe Biden, offering Putin the prospect of an advantageous ceasefire and a return to the international fold.
The U.S.-Iran war this year interrupted momentum but Trump returned to the topic of Ukraine again in October, criticizing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for continuing to attack Russian energy infrastructure, while declaring that Putin’s side had been “fine”.
Fearing the negotiations were drifting toward collapse, Stubb and Støre intervened. Støre hosted Zelenskyy and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo in an attempt to repair relations. Stubb, who also attended, declared the meeting on Oct. 20 had put the peace process “back on track.”
But 24 hours later, Witkoff again stunned European leaders by meeting Putin in St. Petersburg and praising him as a “humanitarian.”
After consulting Zelenskyy, the two Nordic leaders concluded they could not leave Trump, Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner as the only Western figures speaking directly to Putin.
Stubb and Støre have known each other for years and worked closely on Russian affairs when they both served as foreign ministers. They talk and text frequently — and like to pair up on key files despite coming from different political backgrounds.
They had quietly explored the idea of a joint call to the Kremlin for months and concluded that reviving momentum would be critical ahead of renewed negotiations in Abu Dhabi.
Europeans, many officials privately acknowledge, no longer trusted Washington to defend either Europe’s interests or Ukraine’s.
“We have to ask the question in Europe if we feel that someone else should have the contact and the discussion on our behalf,” one EU government official said. “Is the feeling that the U.S. should own our objectives?”
“It’s important that Donald Trump is not the only leader from the West who talks to Putin,” another senior European official said. “We need pro-Ukraine leaders putting their messages to Putin too.”
So, almost five years after Russia’s diplomatic isolation began, Stubb and Støre decided to call the Kremlin. The Nordic team reached out to Putin’s officials and agreed parameters for the conversation. Each side would take turns to deliver their prepared messages, without interruption from the other.
Some of the omens were inauspicious from the start.
As the leaders sat next to each other at the long cabinet table in Stubb’s plush presidential salon on Oct. 27, two large, gilt-framed oil paintings loomed over them, depicting battle scenes from the Crimean War. One canvas shows an Anglo-French naval force retreating under fire on Finnish territory, a reminder of an era two centuries ago when Finland itself was part of the Russian Empire.
According to some accounts, Putin shared his own keen interest in Russia’s past with the two Nordic leaders — delivering a lengthy lesson on Slavic history and the origins of the war in Ukraine.
One senior official familiar with the matter said Stubb and Støre listened patiently during the 90-minute conversation. Other European officials briefed on the call denied that Putin had given the two leaders a history lecture at all, and suggested this claim was Russian spin aimed at humiliating the Europeans.
Støre himself said: “I was present. He didn’t.” Putin has well-worn arguments about the origins of the war, he added. “But in all fairness, he can give his explanation, and we respond to that.”
For their part, the Nordic pair first gave Putin Zelenskyy’s messages — that territorial boundaries can only be discussed at leader level, face to face, and first there must be de-escalation measures. Stubb and his friend then turned to the matter of Baltic Sea security and the need to keep the waterway open for trade.
One reason for holding the call was to try to judge Putin’s state of mind, according to officials. The Norwegian leader said Putin was “rational” and “professional” on the phone. “His arguments were perfectly clearly transmitted.”
Putin took the idea of talks in Abu Dhabi seriously and told the Nordic pair he would instruct his negotiators to prepare for the meeting to explore if progress is possible. “The fact that he picks up that phone, that we have, you know, other ways of reaching, I think that signals, at least that there’s a readiness to sit down.”
But afterwards, Støre was still not convinced that Putin was genuinely open to a deal. Despite their efforts, the Norwegian and Finnish team do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi.
When Stubb’s office announced the surprise call had happened, the diplomatic blowback played out live in public.
By coincidence, the leaders of Denmark and Sweden, among others, were already gathered in Helsinki for a Nordic Council meeting. Confronted by TV crews, they made little effort to hide their irritation.
“I’m very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative,” Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told broadcasters. “I think we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement”. Lithuania also criticized the move.
In private, some diplomats were even harsher. “There are too many middle-aged men who want to end up in the history books having solved this war,” one EU diplomat said. “Putin is just gaining from opening up a more normalized dialogue with the rest of the world — and continuing to bomb and kill i

articles.title_zh: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
articles.content_orig:
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

articles.title_orig: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
articles.title_zh: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
articles.content_orig:
Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquiry looking into the issue has said.
The inquiry's first report, published this summer , concluded that once-in-a-generation reforms were needed to fix a system "not serving the interests of white working-class children".
The next phase will focus on early years children and teenagers aged 14 to 19, aiming for a stronger start at primary school and improving older students' routes through education into successful careers.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "backing" the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".
Inquiry co-chair and former education secretary Baroness Morris said the next phase of the inquiry's work will consider "what needs to be done".
"This isn't just the responsibility of schools but calls for action from across society," she said.
The Independent Inquiry into White Working Class Educational Outcomes was commissioned by the multi-academy trust Star Academies, and is supported by the Department for Education.
It spoke to thousands of young people and their parents, as well as hundreds of teachers.
Education data about white working class pupils was also analysed as part of the year-long review, looking at the 1.25 million young people in England who are white British and in receipt of free school meals.
The inquiry found a growing belief among white working-class families that the current education system does not guarantee future success.
In the summer, the inquiry also acknowledged that the true scale of white working-class disadvantage is "likely to be substantially larger", as the education data they looked at did not include families who were on low incomes but did not receive free school meals.
Since then, all families receiving Universal Credit have become eligible for free school meals .
Under the new phase of the inquiry, practical recommendations for government, schools, colleges and other organisations working with white working-class communities will be developed.
This action will include a research programme looking at the routes taken by teenagers aged 14 to 19, investigating how schools can work with communities to provide clearer pathways into further study and successful employment.
The new phase of the inquiry will also look at how schools can ensure the transition from primary to secondary school builds strong foundations.
"Right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education," Powell said.
"That is why I am backing this independent inquiry to get to the heart of the barriers holding children back - from their first steps into school, through to the opportunities and choices they have as teenagers into further study, training or work."
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to open up new technical routes from age 14 in England over the summer.
The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet".
Currently, nearly a million young people are classed as Neet.
Former minister Alan Milburn's interim report found that children who are not school-ready at aged four or five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet by ages 16 to 17.
A final report by Milburn is expected to set out his recommendations for tackling the issue in the coming weeks.

articles.title_orig: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.title_zh: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.content_orig:
The NASA logo is seen at NASA's Johnson Space Center, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston. Karen Warren/AP hide caption
If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.
The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.
"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."
There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.
The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.
While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.
In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.
"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."
In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.
In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.
FILE - This detail of a July 20, 1969 photo made available by NASA shows astronaut Neil Armstrong reflected in the helmet visor of Buzz Aldrin on the surface of the moon. Neil Armstrong/NASA via AP hide caption
If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.
To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.
During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.
The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.

articles.title_zh: Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials.
The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power.
It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate.
Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said.
He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel.
Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties as a result of the attack, based on an initial assessment, the INA reported.
Al-Zaidi also directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with the relevant authorities in the Kurdish region to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, INA reported.
The attack comes amid heightened regional tensions. A drone strike hit the same facility last year, with no group having claimed responsibility.

articles.title_orig: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.title_zh: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.content_orig:
Days after Republicans faced a series of bruising midterm election losses, President Trump stood by his handling of the economy and the Iran war — but he acknowledged some "bad messaging" on economic issues and said his immigration crackdown was "too tough" at times.
In a sitdown with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat, the president also suggested some top administration officials could be on their way out. One hour later, he announced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would depart her role and be replaced by Stephen Miller.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the interview:
Republicans lost more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats on Tuesday, with some races still uncalled, including in places that Mr. Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago. About 63% of midterm voters disapproved of Mr. Trump's job performance, and 44% said one reason for their vote was to express opposition to him, according to CBS News exit polling.
Asked for his analysis of the midterm losses, Mr. Trump told 60 Minutes that voters "didn't like the war" with Iran or the soaring gas prices that it triggered.
But he said he believes the primary reason for Republicans' losses was that "I was not on the ballot," an explanation he has offered several times in recent days. He suggested his pre-election endorsements and rallies "brought a lot of people … a lot closer to victory."
Ahead of Election Day, the president frequently urged his supporters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." So, what happened?
"I think they didn't vote, really. I think they didn't vote. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative," he said.
Some of the candidates were picked by the president. He endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Lone Star State's bitter GOP Senate primary, and he endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother's South Carolina Senate seat — encouraging her to run for a full term.
Mr. Trump argued that "Cornyn would have lost also."
The president defended his stewardship of the economy in his 60 Minutes sitdown, which came hours after a stronger-than-expected jobs report . He said "the numbers are phenomenal."
"We're doing numbers that have never been done before. 401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich," the president said. Pressed on the fact that not all Americans have large retirement accounts, Mr. Trump responded: "But a lot of people do."
But exit polling shows three-fourths of midterm voters viewed the condition of the economy as either poor or not so good — and 70% of that group voted for Democratic House candidates. Voters were especially concerned about prices of gasoline, food, utilities and healthcare, and two-thirds of voters believed that Mr. Trump's tariff policies hurt the country's economy.
Mr. Trump said the problem is that "we couldn't get the word across."
"I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it?" the president said.
He predicted that Americans are "going to notice it in the next two, three, four months," arguing that his policies will lead to a resurgence of manufacturing jobs.
The morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance argued on social media "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone" — the broadly unpopular Iran war."
Mr. Trump said Vance told him about his plan to write that post, and he responded: "You write what you want." The president said "I don't disagree" with the vice president's diagnosis for why the Republicans lost the midterms, "other than one thing."
"The one thing he left out is — that I would say, and maybe he wouldn't say it, I don't know. I've never asked him really. But, if you had … to do again, would you do it? And that's Iran. Would you go and attack Iran?" he said.
The president said his answer to that question is an "emphatic yes," arguing Iran's conventional military has been degraded and its nuclear program has been set back.
"I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not? But … I have to go with what's right for our country," he said. "If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened."
In a visit to the Oval Office later in the day, Mr. Trump reiterated his view that historians will judge the Iran war more favorably than voters. He pointed out a portrait of Ulysses S. Grant, a former president whose reputation has improved with age .
"I mean, he was very low on the list and now he's much higher on the list," Mr. Trump said. "I think as an example — the fact that I have taken the nuclear weapon away from Iran will not be good, short-term. But long-term, I think it's going to be very important."
Since September, Iran and the U.S. have largely held off from major attacks, though the U.S. launched a set of limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets earlier this week.
Mr. Trump has suggested in recent months that the war could ramp up again after the election, but he has also frequently predicted Iran is interested in striking a deal, and Qatar is mediating a diplomatic push between the two sides. He told 60 Minutes he believes Iran is close to striking a deal, but the outcome of the election "gives them a little bit of a hope certificate."
Asked if he plans to escalate the war now that the midterms are over, the president said: "Well, I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to."
Mr. Trump's victory in 2024 was fueled in part by voters' discontent with the Biden administration's immigration policies. But this year, exit polling shows 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. In battlegrounds like Texas, many Latino voters who shifted to Mr. Trump two years ago pivoted back to Democrats due to concerns about immigration policy .
The president said immigration "both helped and hurt."
"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border," he said.
So, which immigration policies hurt him?
"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."
He continued: "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."
"I think it was too tough," the president said of his deportation policies.
Mr. Trump's plans for the second half of his term aren't clear. On Friday, he replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement strategy. Last year, he pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to conduct at least 3,000 arrests per day .
The president said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats.
Mr. Trump is the wealthiest person to hold the presidency, and his wealth has grown by billions in recent years, fueled partly by his family's cryptocurrency ventures . Polls show many voters believe the president is prioritizing his personal business interests while in office.
Asked about reporting by Forbes that his net worth has soared since he returned to the White House, Mr. Trump said, "So did everyone." (Douthat noted that, unlike Mr. Trump, his net worth hasn't gone up by nearly $3 billion. The president responded, "Well, you should've had stock.")
